title: Stovetop Rice Pudding
subtitle: Creamy, slow-stirred rice in whole milk with vanilla, cooked on the hob
excerpt: Short-grain rice simmered slowly in milk with a split vanilla pod until the grains are very soft and the pudding has thickened to a loose, creamy consistency. Looser and quicker than the baked version.
sourceNotes: The stovetop method produces a looser, creamier result than the oven-baked version and is ready in about 40 minutes compared to 2 hours in the oven. Mrs Beeton gave both methods; the baked version became standard in school canteens during the 20th century, but the hob method is the older technique and gives a noticeably different texture.

content.text: Stovetop rice pudding is the hob method, short-grain rice simmered slowly in milk with a split vanilla pod until the grains are very soft and the pudding is thick and creamy. The result is looser than the baked version: more like a pourable porridge than a set spoonable pudding. Stir every 5 minutes throughout to prevent sticking; the grains cook at the bottom of the pan first and will catch if left.

Put the rinsed rice, milk, sugar, and split vanilla pod into a medium, heavy-bottomed saucepan. Bring slowly to a simmer over a medium-low heat, stirring frequently to stop the milk scorching on the base. Once simmering, reduce the heat to the lowest setting.

Cook over the lowest possible heat for 30 to 40 minutes, stirring every 5 minutes and scraping the base and sides of the pan. The pudding is ready when the rice is completely soft, no bite remaining, and the mixture has thickened to a creamy consistency that holds a line briefly before settling back. It should pour from the spoon in a slow, even stream.

Remove the vanilla pod. Stir in the double cream if using, this softens the flavour and adds a little richness. Taste for sweetness and adjust. Serve hot or warm in deep bowls, with a dusting of nutmeg or a spoonful of jam stirred in.

items.symptom: The rice is sticking and catching on the base
items.cause: The heat is too high, or the pan has a thin base.
items.fix: Reduce the heat further and stir more frequently. A heavy-based saucepan distributes heat more evenly and makes this much less likely.

items.cause: Cooked down too far, or the rice absorbed more milk than expected.
items.fix: Stir in an extra splash of hot milk until you reach the consistency you want.

items.symptom: The rice still has bite after 40 minutes
items.cause: The heat was too low from the start, or the rice was not rinsed.
items.fix: Continue cooking, stirring regularly, until the grains are entirely soft. Add a splash more milk if the pudding is thickening before the rice is done.

content.text: Keeps in the fridge for 2 days, covered. The pudding thickens considerably as it cools. To reheat, tip into a pan and stir over a low heat with a splash of milk until it reaches the right consistency again.
